'''Donald Frederick Hornig''' (March 17, 1920&nbsp;– January 21, 2013) was an American chemist, explosives expert, teacher and presidential science advisor. He served as president of [[Brown University]] from 1970 to 1976.

==Life and career==
Hornig was born in [[Milwaukee, Wisconsin]], the son of Chester Arthur Hornig and Emma Knuth. He attended [[University School of Milwaukee|Milwaukee Country Day School]], then earned his undergraduate degree in chemistry from [[Harvard University]]. He was awarded his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1943, at the age of 23, with a dissertation on ''An Investigation of the Shock Wave Produced by an Explosion in Air''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|114962|name=Donald Frederick Hornig}}</ref> On July 17, 1943, he was married to scientist [[Lilli Hornig]]. The couple had four children together: three girls, Joanna, Ellen, and Leslie, and one boy, Christopher.

After graduating, he started work at the Underwater Explosives Laboratory of the [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute]]. While there, according to one obituary, he received an invitation to begin a new job, but he was not told what his duties would be, nor, initially, to where he would relocate. At first he refused, but Harvard University President [[James B. Conant]] helped persuade him to reconsider.<ref name=nyt/> Thus, he joined the [[Los Alamos Laboratory]], where he was a group leader in the [[Manhattan Project]]. He worked on the firing unit that was used for the implosion of the plutonium device.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Alvarez |first1=Luis |title=Alvarez: Adventures of a Physicist |date=1987 |publisher=Basic Books, Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0465001157 |page=136}}</ref> He helped prepare the first atomic bomb, [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity]], and witnessed its explosion, the first detonation of a nuclear device. He was sent up to the top of the tower twice the previous day to reassure a nervous [[Robert Oppenheimer]] that all was well<ref name=nyt>[https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/27/science/donald-hornig-a-bomb-scientist-and-brown-president-dies-at-92.html?ref=obituaries&_r=0 Donald Hornig, Last to See First A-Bomb, Dies at 92], The New York Times, January 26, 2013</ref> and after working on the high voltage capacitors that fire the multiple detonators, he was the last man to leave the tower.<ref>{{cite book |last=Szasz |first=Ferenc Morton |title=The Day the Sun Rose Twice: The Story of the Trinity Site Nuclear Explosion, July 16, 1945 |publisher=UNM Press |year=1984 |isbn=0-8263-0768-X |oclc=10779209 |location=Albuquerque |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/daysunrosetwic00szas}}</ref>

In 1946 he joined the staff of [[Brown University]] as an assistant professor, and became a full professor in 1951. From 1951 to 1952 he was associate dean of the graduate school, then acting dean the following year. In 1957 he became a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and the same year he moved to [[Princeton University]] in 1957. Later became chairman of the Princeton chemistry department.<ref>{{cite web|author=Staff|url=https://www.brown.edu/Administration/President/links/presidents/hornig.html|title=Donald Hornig|publisher=Brown University|accessdate=2008-05-27}}</ref>

Shortly before President [[John F. Kennedy]] was assassinated in 1963, he announced Hornig as the presidential science advisor. Hornig assumed office on January 24, 1964, but did not get along with the new president, [[Lyndon Baines Johnson]], who had poor relationships with many scientists.<ref name=nyt/> He left office at the end of the president's term in 1969, and accepted an executive position with [[Eastman Kodak Company]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Boffey|first=Philip M.|date=January 31, 1969|title=The Hornig Years: Did LBJ Neglect His Science Advisor?|journal=Science|volume=163|issue=3866|pages=453–458|doi=10.1126/science.163.3866.453|pmid=17731760|bibcode=1969Sci...163..453B|issn=0036-8075}}</ref>

In 1970 he became president of [[Brown University]], and he remained in office until he resigned in 1976. The end of his term was noted for financial cutbacks at the university, which was met by student protests. Thereafter he became Professor of Chemistry in Public Health at Harvard University. From 1987 to 1990 he served the Harvard University School of Public Health as chairman of the Department of Environmental Health. He retired in 1990.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sciencepolicy.colorado.edu/scienceadvisors/hornig.html|title=Dr. Donald Hornig|publisher=Colorado University-Boulder|accessdate=2008-05-27}}</ref>

Since 2013, Hornig has been listed on the Advisory Council of the [[National Center for Science Education]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |title=Advisory Council |website=ncse.com |publisher=[[National Center for Science Education]] |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130810112828/https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |archivedate=2013-08-10 |accessdate=2018-10-30|date=2008-07-15 }}</ref>

Hornig died from [[Alzheimer's disease]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.physicstoday.org/1.2907606 |title=American Institute of Physics |access-date=2013-04-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130616005450/http://www.physicstoday.org/1.2907606 |archive-date=2013-06-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> in [[Providence, Rhode Island]], on January 21, 2013.<ref>{{cite news |last=Morgan |first=Thomas J. |url=http://news.providencejournal.com/breaking-news/2013/01/donald-f-hornig-dies-was-president-of-brown-university.html |title=Donald F. Hornig dies; was president of Brown University |department=Breaking News |publisher=The Providence Journal |date=2013-01-22 |accessdate=2013-07-23 |archive-date=2013-07-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130728004228/http://news.providencejournal.com/breaking-news/2013/01/donald-f-hornig-dies-was-president-of-brown-university.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==In popular culture==
In the 1989 film ''[[Fat Man and Little Boy (film)|Fat Man and Little Boy]]'', directed by [[Roland Joffé]], Hornig was portrayed by actor [[Jim True-Frost]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Catalog - Fat Man and Little Boy |url=https://catalog.afi.com/Catalog/moviedetails/58066 |website=[[AFI Catalog]] |access-date=July 16, 2025}}</ref>

In the 2023 film ''[[Oppenheimer (film)|Oppenheimer]]'', directed by [[Christopher Nolan]], Hornig was portrayed by actor [[David Rysdahl]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Neal |last=Justin |title=New Ulm native David Rysdahl helped 'Fargo' co-stars nail the accent |url=https://www.startribune.com/new-ulm-native-david-rysdahl-helped-fargo-co-stars-nail-the-accent/600321161 |website=[[Star Tribune]] |date=November 20, 2023 |access-date=July 16, 2025|url-status=live |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250510190104/https://www.startribune.com/new-ulm-native-david-rysdahl-helped-fargo-co-stars-nail-the-accent/600321161 |archive-date=May 10, 2025}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* Winner of the [[Charles Lathrop Parsons Award]] of the [[American Chemical Society]], 1967.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://portal.acs.org/portal/acs/corg/content?_nfpb=true&_pageLabel=PP_ARTICLEMAIN&node_id=1319&content_id=CTP_004498&use_sec=true&sec_url_var=region1|title=Charles Lathrop Parsons Award|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=2008-05-27}}</ref>
* Honorary LL.D from Boston College, November 12, 1966.<ref>{{cite web|author=President's Office|date=August 5, 1996|url=http://www.bc.edu/publications/factbook/meta-elements/html/fb97honor_dg_recip.html|title=Honorary Degrees Awarded by Boston College 1952-1995|publisher=Boston College|accessdate=2008-05-27|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070915084904/http://www.bc.edu/publications/factbook/meta-elements/html/fb97honor_dg_recip.html|archivedate=September 15, 2007}}</ref>
* Honorary D.Sc. from the University of Maryland, 1965.<ref>{{cite web|author=Staff|date=June 19, 2006|url=http://www.lib.umd.edu/univarchives/macmil/honorarydegrees1.html|title=Honorary Degrees|publisher=University of Maryland Libraries|accessdate=2008-05-27}}</ref>
* Honorary D.Sc. from Syracuse University, 1968.<ref>{{cite web|author=Staff|year=2008|url=http://archives.syr.edu/awards/honorary_2.html|title=Recipient of Honorary Degrees|publisher=Archives and Records Management, Syracuse University|accessdate=2008-05-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100609172315/http://archives.syr.edu/awards/honorary_2.html|archive-date=2010-06-09|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].
* Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].
* Member of the [[American Philosophical Society]].
* Recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship.
* Recipient of a Fulbright Fellowship.
